item.title: Elon Musk's power now extends far beyond Tesla, and Ukraine shows why
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Elon Musk's influence over first Tesla ( TSLA ) and now SpaceX ( SPCX ) has long been measured in terms of corporate valuations, technological breakthroughs, and personal wealth, where his companies have made him the richest person in the world. Across the last few years, however, the centi-billionaire's growing portfolio of businesses has pushed him into a new lane entirely. Over the past decade, Elon Musk has become far more than a corporate executive or political power broker. Through his control of companies underpinning global communications, military operations, space access, and artificial intelligence, Musk has acquired a degree of influence over national security, international relations, and the global economy that few private individuals have ever possessed. An artilleryman of the Special Rifle Police Battalion of Zaporizhzhia region sets up Starlink satellite internet system, at a position, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, near the frontline in Donetsk region, Ukraine, October 16, 2026. REUTERS/Stringer/File Photo Reuters / REUTERS "There's a very real chance that [Musk] is the most powerful civilian, non-governmental actor in history," Gautam Mukunda, a research fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School and managing director of the consultancy Two Rivers Group. Musk "has resources that are vastly larger than those of all but a handful of governments on the planet." That influence came into sharp focus this month when widely reported restrictions on SpaceX's satellite communications services disrupted Ukraine's military operations, exposing just how dependent a sovereign nation's battlefield capabilities had become on infrastructure supplied by a private-sector company. There are conflicting accounts of who ordered the restrictions in Ukraine, which disrupted battlefield drones and prompted several hours of faltering drone speeds and faulty communications on the front lines of the nation's conflict with Russia. Musk says the White House controls Ukraine's access to Starshield, a military-grade version of Starlink funded by the Pentagon, while officials in the Trump administration have said they weren't involved in the decision . Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS. Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities… — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 14, 2026 Regardless of responsibility, the incident has highlighted the increasing separation between corporate access to governments and governmental reliance on the private sector, particularly given Musk's singular control over rocketry and satellite communications. 'Extraordinary power' SpaceX is now responsible for roughly 90% of all mass sent into orbit off Earth, Musk said on SpaceX's recent earnings call. The Pentagon is Starshield's largest customer , while countries such as the Philippines , Argentina , and Indonesia use Starlink for national communications, including emergency services. "He can turn a country's communications on or off — that's an extraordinary power," Darrell West, senior fellow at the Brookings Institution's Center for Technology Innovation, told Yahoo Finance. "Even governments can't do that." To be sure, Musk is far from the only corporate leader to have garnered significant political power. CEOs of the largest banks in the world, like JPMorgan Chase's ( JPM ) Jamie Dimon and Goldman Sachs' ( GS ) David Solomon, have repeatedly spoken with or alongside the US president. Oil and gas majors like ExxonMobil ( XOM ) under Darren Woods and Chevron ( CVX ) under Mike Wirth have made deals with war-torn nations such as Libya and Iraq in search of cheap and sizeable fossil fuel deposits. Perhaps most visibly over the last year, Silicon Valley's largest leaders have become increasingly common sights in Washington, D.C., attending dinners and state summits at the White House and pushing AI legislation in the halls of Congress. When Trump hosted China's Xi Jinping at the White House in late September, Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO Jensen Huang, OpenAI's ( OPAI.PVT ) Sam Altman, Microsoft ( MSFT ) CEO Satya Nadella, and Amazon ( AMZN ) CEO Jeff Bezos were all in attendance alongside Musk. Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell, and NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang attend the "A New Golden Age" summit at the US Institute of Peace, renamed The Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace by the Trump administration, in Washington, DC, US, October 8, 2026. REUTERS/Evan Vucci REUTERS / REUTERS But Musk's dominance across several industries critical to national security — including but not limited to space communications, rocketry, and advanced robotics — have placed him in a singular category of corporate-driven geopolitical power. More broadly, the Starlink-Ukraine fallout underscores a broader transformation underway in the global economy: Technologies once controlled, developed, or operated primarily by governments are increasingly concentrated in the hands of a small number of corporations, giving their executives considerable influence over international affairs. The US government has the capacity for major strategic projects, such as the invention of the atomic bomb through the Manhattan Project in the 1940s or the first moon landing in 1969. Yet the state has instead chosen to outsource much of that ability to private corporations that have garnered immense power and reliance, Adam Segal, the Council on Foreign Relations' Ira A. Lipman Chair in Emerging Technologies and National Security, told Yahoo Finance. China's President Xi Jinping (L) and US President Donald Trump speak through interpreters as First Lady Melania Trump listens to Tesla CEO Elon Musk during a State Dinner in the East Room of the White House in Washington, DC, on September 24, 2026. (Brendan SMIALOWSKI / AFP via Getty Images) BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI via Getty Images "There are probably some national security areas where we want to ensure that NASA can still do this, but I think that's going to be pretty narrow," Segal said. He added, "The idea that the Pentagon and the government more broadly is just going to be reliant on commercial tech because it's going to be the most advanced, that is going to be very hard to put back in the bottle." Musk's growing state-adjacent power also comes as geopolitics have begun to play an increasingly visible role in market performance, driving everything from oil prices and global sovereign debt yields to Big Tech equity performance. The war in Iran has disrupted global energy flows and pushed up inflation across developed economies; protests in France have depressed bond prices across the eurozone; Nvidia's reliance on chips from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing ( TSM ) has thrust increasingly fractious relations between Beijing and Taipei back into the spotlight. CEO of Microsoft Satya Nadella, Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell, AMD CEO Lisa Su, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang, and Google co-founder Sergey Brin stand with U.S. President Donald Trump during the "A New Golden Age" summit at the US Institute of Peace, renamed The Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace by the Trump administration, in Washington, DC, US, October 8, 2026. REUTERS/Evan Vucci REUTERS / REUTERS The Ukraine-Russia war, where Musk has been most visibly in focus, has directly contributed to the diesel price crisis facing the US. The disruptions to the Ukrainian military's use of Starshield come as the White House has offered the Kremlin incentives and concessions that have included allowing the sale of Russian energy products on the open market, breaking with years of US sanctions on Moscow. "2026 has seen economists and strategists forced to accept that geopolitics, rather than being the odd exogenous shock, is a structural backdrop disrupting models and markets," Rabobank global strategist Michael Every said. "Changing politics can also change markets." For investors in SpaceX and Tesla, geopolitics — and Musk's influence over some of the most critical global developments — have become an increasingly large part of the Musk story, at times eclipsing the traditional financial metrics used to judge the performance of a corporate executive. Teams inside SpaceX and Tesla are reportedly pursuing an aggressive timeline to merge the two companies before the 2028 presidential election while friendly faces remain in the White House. Senator Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) said Thursday that Congress should issue subpoenas to Elon Musk, Starlink/SpaceX, and the Department of Defense over interference in Ukraine. Musk responded publicly to reports of a potential investigation on Wednesday. "Live by the sword, die by the sword," Musk said on X . "Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets." item.title: Pastor Adam Hamilton could be Kansas's 1st Democratic senator since the Depression
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
When it comes to picking senators, no state is nearly as consistent as Kansas. The last Democrat to win there, a former county attorney named George McGill, was elected in 1932. Kansas's other senator, a Republican incumbent, won reelection in 1936. McGill lost to a Republican in 1938. And Kansas has been sending Republicans to the U.S. Senate ever since. That's a 90-year winning streak. But the composition of Kansas's Senate delegation could change on Nov. 3 — and with it, Republican control of the chamber as a whole. To the surprise of pretty much the entire political world, first-term GOP incumbent Roger Marshall is currently locked in a too-close-to-call contest with megachurch-pastor-turned-rookie-candidate Adam Hamilton — a former Republican who considered running as an independent before deciding to seek the Sunflower State's Democratic nomination. Hamilton, 61, is one of several heartland Democrats or Democratic-leaning independents who are giving Senate Republicans a run for their money in ruby-red states that President Trump won by double-digit margins in 2024 (including Texas, Iowa, Nebraska and even South Carolina ). He describes himself as " a liberal conservative and a conservative liberal ." "I'm not somebody who favors the Socialist Party," Hamilton said Wednesday night during a debate against Marshall. "I'm somebody who stands in the middle. I'm going to try to work for all Kansans, Republicans, independents and Democrats." Here's everything you need to know about one of the key figures of the 2026 midterms. Yahoo Who is Adam Hamilton? In some ways, Hamilton is similar to James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee in Texas , who is equally unapologetic about his Christian faith. But where Talarico has studied at seminary on the side — his main gig has been serving in the Texas House of Representatives — Hamilton is a bona fide church leader. Born in 1964 and raised in the Kansas City suburb of Prairie Village, Hamilton didn't go to church regularly as a child. His parents were teenage high school dropouts when they had him; they divorced by the time he was a teenager. Hamilton started drinking and taking drugs in seventh grade; two years later he got clean and started attending Pentecostal services on the recommendation of a door-to-door evangelist. Before long, Hamilton was heading up the church's youth group; he married a fellow attendee a week after high school graduation. Eventually, he earned a bachelor's degree in pastoral ministry from Oral Roberts University in Tulsa and a Master of Divinity from Southern Methodist University in Dallas. In 1990 — when Hamilton was just 25 — his United Methodist denomination tapped him to start a church for nonchurchgoers in suburban Kansas City. Worshippers initially met in the small chapel of a local funeral home. Today, Hamilton's United Methodist Church of the Resurrection is the largest United Methodist congregation in the U.S., with an average weekly attendance of about 25,000 people online, on television and across its nine area campuses. Its Christmas Eve offering, which is devoted to mission work, has topped $2 million . Hamilton has also written more than 30 books that have together sold millions of copies; his video-based lessons are used in Sunday school classes nationwide. In 2013, he preached at the National Prayer Service after President Barack Obama's second inauguration. Three years later, Obama appointed Hamilton to his Advisory Council on Faith-Based and Neighborhood Partnerships. Hamilton was registered as a Republican as recently as 2020; when he was first considering a 2026 Senate bid, he formed an exploratory committee as an independent. At the time he told his congregation — "a nearly equal mix of Republicans, Democrats and Independents," according to the Associated Press — that he could "bridge partisan divides in a highly polarized political climate" (as the AP put it). "Every week, it seemed there was another news story in the last year where I would find myself shaking my head and thinking, we have to do better," the self-described fifth-generation Kansan told the AP. But Hamilton was persuaded to run as a Democrat so as not to split the anti-Marshall vote in the general election. He wound up massively outraising his Democratic primary opponents and winning the party's Aug. 4 primary by more than 20 percentage points . What does Hamilton stand for? In college, Hamilton chose not to become a Pentecostal preacher because the denomination felt too black and white. In contrast, Methodism struck him as a thinking person's church, he told a local Kansas City paper in 2002 . "It seemed to me there was some gray in the world," Hamilton explained. "It is OK if you have doubts. It's OK if you have questions. We don't have to check our brains at the door." He now says he is an "independent-minded Democrat" who is "going to work across the aisle." At the Wednesday debate, Hamilton criticized Marshall for supporting the Trump administration's least-popular policies — tariffs, the war in Iran, immigration raids in farm country — while trying to distance himself from national Democrats. He called former President Joe Biden's immigration policy a "disaster," for instance, and promised not to "support Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader if the Democrats [were] to control the Senate." When asked about transgender girls playing women's sports, Hamilton said he would not want his 12-year-old granddaughter competing against people assigned male at birth. "It's not a fair fight," he argued. Hamilton, left, and Republican Sen. Roger Marshall participate in a debate at WDAF TV in Kansas City, Mo. on Oct. 21, 2026. Charlie Riedel/AP via AP At times, Hamilton — who reminded the audience that he has "been a pastor for the last 38 years" and has "not been a senator" — struggled to provide specifics on issues such as farm subsidies, the Social Security wage cap and AI regulation, according to the New York Times . But Hamilton's general approach — his focus on "decency," affordability and "bringing people together" — has its roots in his ministry. Following the recent surge of federal immigration agents to Minneapolis, he cited on his podcast an Old Testament verse that commands Israelites to treat foreigners with love and fairness. In April, he said that he had voted against a state constitutional amendment that would have cleared the way for tougher abortion restrictions, arguing lawmakers should not be "the ethicists and the spiritual guides" for women (even as he lamented that his mother considered having an abortion when she was pregnant with him). And he has criticized Republican cuts to federal safety-net programs such as food stamps and Medicaid. "I just want to know, when did it become 'woke' to care for your neighbor?" Hamilton asked the AP , claiming that "Marshall would call [Jesus] 'woke'" if he were alive today. How could Hamilton perform in the midterms? Hamilton's local prominence, fundraising prowess, "centrist" message and skill on the stump have made this year's Kansas Senate contest very competitive. ("No one has more practice at extemporaneous talking than a megachurch pastor," the Times noted.) Marshall leads by 1 percentage point in the most recent poll to be released — but it's the only survey conducted over the last month that shows the Republican candidate ahead. The rest (save one tie) give Hamilton a slight edge (between 1 and 5 percentage points). Both candidates have faced controversy. Marshall has pushed back on reports that he sued hundreds of patients over unpaid medical bills during his decades-long career as an obstetrician-gynecologist, calling the allegations "blatant lies." And Hamilton has admitted he made a "mistake" by failing to bar a volunteer who had previously been accused of sexual abuse in 2005 from going on a retreat where he allegedly abused another boy. "I was actually preaching that weekend at Church of the Resurrection, and I did not sign off on him going back. I should have checked to make sure that he wasn't going back," Hamilton said during Wednesday's debate. "That was a mistake on my part. But I will tell you, when he was investigated the next year, we forbade him from working with youth or children anymore. He left our church angry and upset. And again, we played a critical role several years later in getting him arrested and convicted." Kansas hasn't sent a Democratic senator to Washington, D.C., since the Dust Bowl days — a conservative bent that's also reflected in its heavily Republican state legislature and the fact that it has voted Republican in every presidential election since 1940 except for Lyndon B. Johnson's 1964 landslide. But the state has elected two Democratic governors in recent years — Kathleen Sebelius (2003-2009) and term-limited incumbent Laura Kelly (2019-2027) — and there is a tradition of ticket-splitting that goes back even further. (Since 1957, neither major political party has held the Kansas governor's mansion for longer than eight consecutive years.) Could Hamilton benefit from that sort of checks-and-balances heterodoxy on Nov. 3? It's possible. In Wednesday's debate, Marshall embraced the Trump agenda and explicitly told viewers that "if you want [it] to continue, you need to come out, because we delivered on those things." But even in Kansas, 53% of likely voters currently disapprove of how the president is handling his job . The fate of Hamilton's campaign, and perhaps his party's hopes of winning the Senate, will turn on whether he can convince those voters to cast their ballots for him on Election Day — even if they haven't voted for a Democrat in a long, long time. item.title: Tanker carrying Russian diesel heads to U.S. for first time since 2022 under Trump deal
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Oct 23 (Reuters) - The first Russian diesel bound for the US following a surprise agreement reached between Moscow and US President Donald Trump is aboard a tanker heading for New York, ship-tracking data showed on ‌Friday. Trump announced the deal this month as part of his efforts to bring down soaring diesel prices ahead ‌of November 3 US mid-term elections. Trump also waived parts of a new US sanctions law against Russia and threatened Europe with a US diesel export ​ban unless countries released more from their emergency reserves to help ease prices. The Malta-flagged medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes was loaded with 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low sulphur diesel in Russia's Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22, according to LSEG shipping data. It is expected to arrive in the United States on November 7. The identity of the buyer and seller were not immediately known. The ‌cargo will be the first imported by ⁠the US since former President Joe Biden announced a ban on US imports of Russian oil and petroleum products in 2022. Trump announced on October 9 that Russia would immediately export 300,000 metric ⁠tons, or 2.25 million barrels, to the US and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter". A Kremlin spokesperson on Friday confirmed a first ship under the deal had departed, but did not specify whether it was bound for the ​US market ​or elsewhere. "As far as I'm aware, there have already been reports ​from the Ministry of Energy that the first ‌tanker has, in fact, set sail for its recipients, its buyers. Further shipments will continue at a steady pace from here on," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on a daily conference call. The deal with the US involved Russia lifting a self-imposed ban on diesel exports. RUSSIA RESUMING GLOBAL EXPORTS Since the EU imposed a full embargo on imports of Russian oil products in February 2023 over the war in Ukraine, Russia has exported diesel mainly to Turkey and Brazil, as well as to African ‌countries. It also supplies Central Asia by rail. Shipping data from LSEG and Kpler ​published this week showed Russian diesel cargoes resuming voyages to their traditional ​destinations after Moscow lifted its own ban, with at ​least two tankers signalling trips to Turkey and Brazil. It was unclear where other tankers were destined ‌for, with cargoes loaded in Primorsk signalling Gibraltar, the ​Atlantic Coast or Port-Said, LSEG ​data showed. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak has said additional US shipments would follow as companies from the two countries work out the necessary contracts. Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who also heads Russia's sovereign wealth fund, said last week ​that the US Treasury had asked the ‌fund to help sort out tricky payment issues relating to the agreement. Novak has said that Russia would ​be able to increase its diesel exports to its usual levels of 3-3.5 million tons per month by ​year-end. (Reporting by Reuters; editing by Philippa Fletcher and Jason Neely) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://uk.finance.yahoo.com/news/exclusive-tanker-carrying-40-000-062736177.html

item.title: First-of-its-kind cancer vaccine cuts risk of melanoma returning by 42% in major trial
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — A first-of-its-kind cancer vaccine is significantly reducing the chances that melanoma patients’ tumors come back, according to results of a major study released Thursday by drugmakers Moderna and Merck. The vaccine was custom-brewed for each patient to match their tumor. Adding it to a standard post-surgery treatment reduced by 42% the risk of melanoma returning two years after surgery, according to the most advanced study to date of this new strategy for fighting cancer. “The field has been looking for a win and I think this one is a big one,” said Dr. Hussein Tawbi of MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, one of the researchers in the international study. The vaccine, called intismeran, is made with the same Nobel Prize-winning mRNA technology that was behind COVID-19 vaccines. Experimental personalized cancer vaccines made with mRNA and some other approaches also are being tested against other types of cancer including lung, kidney and pancreatic. Experts not involved with the new study say its success bolsters the field. “This is a new frontier,” said Karen Knudsen, CEO of the Parker Institute, which helps fund cancer immunotherapy research. “It’s a big step forward for science, for oncology, because this vaccine will apply to many different cancers,” said Dr. Michael Atkins, deputy director of Georgetown University’s Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center. Moderna and Merck had announced in August that the late-stage trial of intismeran was successful but the detailed results were set to be released Saturday at a meeting of the European Society of Medical Oncology in Madrid. Some of the data was leaked publicly late Thursday, prompting a full release ahead of the weekend's scientific presentation. Most people think of vaccines as preventing an infection, like measles or whooping cough. There are already two cancer-preventing vaccines, the HPV and hepatitis B shots that block infection from those tumor-causing viruses. And research is underway to prevent some types of inherited cancer such as Lynch syndrome-caused colorectal cancer. But a personalized vaccine designed to block surgically-removed cancer from returning is very different. For the intismeran study, scientists hunted gene mutations unique to each patient’s tumor, mutations that create proteins which shouldn’t be in the body unless those cancer cells start to grow again. The custom vaccine — nine doses given three weeks apart — teaches the patient’s immune system to watch out for and attack those so-called neoantigens. How did it work? The study included more than 1,100 people with high-risk melanoma that was surgically removed. Everyone was given the standard follow-up therapy: Merck’s immunotherapy named Keytruda. The participants were randomly assigned to also receive custom-brewed vaccine doses or a placebo. Two years later, 82% of the people in the vaccine group were still living without a recurrence of their cancer compared to 70% who had gotten standard Keytruda alone. The trial is continuing to track participants’ longer-term outcomes. JERUSALEM (AP) — Two Israeli soldiers were killed in an attack in the occupied West Bank on Friday morning that also left two suspected gunmen dead, the military said, violence that is likely to heighten political tensions and security concerns ahead of Israel’s parliamentary election next week. The army said two soldiers, Staff Sgt. Ron Yonatan Roytman, 23, and Sgt. Yuval Shai Svilem, 20, were killed and three others were lightly wounded during an attack by Palestinian gunmen. The attack took place near the Yehuda Junction outside the West Bank city of Hebron. The army said it had prevented a “terror attack against Israeli civilians” and that the two suspects, both Palestinians from Hebron, were armed with an M16 rifle and a handgun. It said the men arrived at an Israeli military position in the morning, triggering an exchange of fire lasting approximately 20 minutes, after which the gunmen were killed by Israeli troops. The army said its forces prevented the men from advancing further where the attack could have resulted in civilian casualties. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office later said it had instructed security forces to immediately cordon off Hebron and prepare for a full closure of the West Bank, starting Friday. During a visit to the site of the attack on Friday, the prime minister said Israel would retaliate with a sweeping anti-terror operation in the Hebron neighborhood where the gunmen had resided. “We will evacuate the residents, we will go house by house, we will also remove the weapons there, and all the terror infrastructure will be dealt with and destroyed,” Netanyahu said. Israeli voters will decide next Tuesday whether to grant Netanyahu yet another term in office — or usher in a new era of Israeli politics. The election comes three years after the Hamas-led attacks on Israel that triggered the war in Gaza. Israel’s government has warned of potential attacks by the country’s “enemies” in the lead-up to the election. Netanyahu holds an emergency meeting Netanyahu later met with his Security Cabinet and officials from top military and security agencies in an emergency meeting, blaming Hamas for Friday's attack. “Our brave soldiers thwarted this attack with courage and determination,” he said, without elaborating on what the planned attack entailed. “I commend them for their actions and wish our wounded a speedy recovery,” he added. Earlier in the day, Israel’s far-right national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, known for extremist views , said that the attack shows that Israel needs to restrict the Palestinians’ freedom of movement in the West Bank. “The lives of the residents of Judea and Samaria, of the settlers, the lives of the soldiers, the lives of the police officers, the lives of our fighters are a million times more important than freedom of movement,” he said, using an Israeli reference to the West Bank. item.title: Supreme Court sides with Republicans in New Hampshire student ID voting fight
item.description:

WASHINGTON – The Supreme Court said New Hampshire can fully enforce a ban on voters using student IDs as a form of identification at the polls next month, a win for the Republican Party's effort to tighten voting procedures. The court on Oct. 22 agreed to pause a lower court’s ruling that a student ID is among the forms of identification that may be considered by poll workers if the voter lacks an approved government-issued ID. The state's U.S. Senate race is among the contests that will decide whether Republicans keep control of that chamber after the midterm elections. The Republican National Committee had backed the state's unsuccessful emergency appeal to the Supreme Court . New Hampshire, controlled by Republicans, is among several states that have banned registered voters from using a student ID to verify their identity at the polls. A voting-rights group challenged the change as discrimination against younger voters and as an unconstitutional burden on their right to vote. A federal judge in New Hampshire declined to block enforcement of the law as the case is litigated. But the judge also said the new law had not changed the fact that a poll worker may accept or reject a student ID as a valid form of identification on a case-by-case basis through the state’s "safety-valve" provision. New Hampshire Secretary of State David Scanlan asked the Supreme Court to intervene. Scanlan, a Republican, said the judge's Oct. 2 order injected uncertainty into the state’s voting procedures less than three weeks before the election. He also said the judge wrongly interpreted the state's law. Coalition for Open Democracy, the group challenging the law, said the judge correctly concluded that state officials failed to identify "any security or integrity concerns specific to student ID cards and why they are unique among other non-governmental forms of identification" that are allowed on a case-by-case basis. The judge also found that the change had already kept one student from voting and could affect more because young voters may not have the government-issued IDs that are automatically accepted. In the brief and unsigned opinion, the Supreme Court pointed to its previous rulings that federal courts should not alter rules on the eve of an election. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only justice to publicly disagree with that decision. She said the federal judge had not changed the rules but only corrected the secretary of state's misinterpretation of them. "I respectfully dissent because − even, and perhaps especially, when an election is looming − I would not disturb aclearly justifiable federal-court order issued to ensure that the public receives accurate information about a State'selectoral processes," she wrote. item.title: Meta struck an unusual deal to keep Mark Zuckerberg from leaving California
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Meta Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg has made a deal with the firm's board allowing him to sell or transfer up to 20% of the company's new Class C stock so that his voting majority doesn't decrease even if he has to pay the billionaire tax. (Nic Coury / Associated Press ) Meta’s Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg has wielded enormous power over the social media empire he built more than two decades ago, leading the California juggernaut through major scandals, scrutiny and technological shifts. But the 42-year-old tech mogul considered leaving the state because he feared that a ballot measure to impose a one-time 5% tax on the assets of California billionaires could reduce the amount of control he has over Meta, a recent regulatory filing shows. Meta’s board struck a deal so he would stay in California. Meta is the parent company of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. The filing highlights how one of the world’s wealthiest people, whose net worth totals more than $200 billion, is bracing for the possibility that California voters pass Proposition 40, a wealth tax proposal that would primarily be used to fund healthcare. Although supporters say the fear that billionaires will flee the state are overblown, the ultrawealthy have made moves to potentially avoid paying the tax or are funding campaigns to defeat it. Read more: Your guide to Proposition 40: California's billionaire tax proposal Zuckerberg’s influence over Meta is partly tied to how the company structures its stock. Zuckerberg holds roughly 60% of voting power over Meta even though he only owns about 13% of the company’s total shares. Meta has a dual-class share structure, dividing the stock into Class A shares with one vote each and Class B shares with 10 votes each. Zuckerberg holds a large amount of Class B stock, which gives him majority control over company decisions. If the wealth tax proposal passes, Zuckerberg is worried that it could reduce his voting power, according to the filing. The tech executive makes an annual salary of $1, so most of his wealth is linked to his stake in Meta. If he had to sell his Class B shares to pay the tax, that would reduce his voting majority in the company, according to the filing. In September, he told Meta’s board that he planned to list his Palo Alto home for sale, pressuring board members to find a solution. On Wednesday, Meta announced a new class of stock with no voting rights called Class C that would take effect in January. As part of the deal, Zuckerberg could sell or transfer up to 20% of Class C stock so his voting majority doesn’t decrease even if he has to pay the tax. “Mr. Zuckerberg’s continued leadership role in our Company, and his continuing presence at the Company’s headquarters in California, is critical at this current inflection point for the Company and the tech industry in order to continue to provide value-maximization for all shareholders,” the filing said. Since the company’s public debut, its share price has risen more than 1,700%, outperforming the S&P 500. In Meta’s third-quarter earnings call Wednesday, Chief Financial Officer Susan Li said creating a new class of nonvoting stock benefits the company in various ways, including “capital raising, employee compensation, acquisitions, other general corporate purposes.” “We believe this share class will maintain our founder-led structure. It will expand our funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we’re seeing across every part of our business driven by AI,” she said. Meta has roughly 66,700 workers globally. Its sprawling headquarters is in Menlo Park. Some billionaires such as Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey, Ripple co-founder Chris Larsen and Google co-founder Sergey Brin have opposed the wealth tax proposal. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, on the other hand, has said he doesn’t mind paying more taxes. The Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West is backing the wealth tax proposal and says it applies to roughly 200 billionaires who have resided in California as of January 1, 2026, and could raise $100 billion. More than $300 million has been contributed to fight the billionaire tax, including two propositions that could block it if they gather more votes. Although stock prices fluctuate, Zuckerberg could face a tax liability of roughly $12 billion based on his net worth. In 2015, Zuckerberg and his wife, Dr. Priscilla Chan, pledged to give away 99% of his Facebook shares over their lifetimes when they celebrated the birth of their first daughter. The couple created the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, a philanthropic organization whose efforts include curing, managing and preventing all diseases. item.title: Trump tells Ramaswamy to keep using attack ad featuring rival's estranged mother
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Washington — President Trump on Thursday praised the "very powerful ad" Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy is running featuring the estranged mother of Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, after the ad drew pushback from some Republicans like Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine. Mr. Trump posted on Truth Social that he suggested Ramaswamy keep the ad up, saying the press is "trying to convince everyone that this Ad is bad, because it's so good!" The ad , which first circulated on social media on Monday and is now television, features Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur, who called Acton a "liar" and sought to undermine her credibility. Acton's campaign condemned the ad, and her brother, Philip Stearns, called it a "despicable low." According to court documents provided by the campaign, Arthur's now-deceased husband was charged with raping Acton, which she said occurred when she was between 10 and 12 years old. He entered a not guilty plea and left the area while out on bond; the case never went to trial. DeWine on Thursday said he thought the Ramaswamy campaign should take the ad down . "It's wrong to run this ad," the Ohio Republican told reporters. "I would urge Ramaswamy's campaign to take this down." DeWine did not rescind his endorsement. But Vice President JD Vance and now Mr. Trump are defending the ad and using it to criticize Acton. "Vivek Ramaswamy put up a very powerful Ad about a mother saying that her daughter, Amy Acton, who is running for Governor of Ohio, is a liar, and much worse," Mr. Trump wrote in his social media post. "The Press, in a concerted and well coordinated attack, is trying to get Vivek Ramaswamy to 'take down the Ad.' Frankly, anybody whose mother spoke about a daughter in that way would normally lead to the daughter being precluded from serving in Office, let alone the Office of Governor." In his post, Mr. Trump did not mention why Acton and her birth mother are estranged, or any of the family's backstory. Shortly after his post, on the White House South Lawn, reporters told Mr. Trump the backstory — that Acton's mother stayed married to the man charged with raping her. CBS News senior White House reporter Weijia Jiang asked the president why anyone should listen to what the estranged mother has to say. "Well I know nothing about it," the president responded. "All I know is the mother said very bad things about Acton, who I guess is running for governor against Vivek. And all I can say is Vivek is great. And I know one thing, if my mother said bad about me, it would be a major news story, that's for sure. So I don't know what it is, but I guess the mother said very bad things about the one who's running for governor. And I think you have to say that seriously." "I'm defending it because I know that if that ad were about my mother, you would love it, you would love every inch of it," Mr. Trump added. In his Truth Social post, the president specifically went after DeWine. "Our RINO Governor of Ohio, Mike DeWine, who I unfortunately helped get elected years ago, when he was losing by 16 points prior to my doing a Rally for him was, as usual, disloyal to the Republican Party," Mr. Trump wrote. "He strongly suggested that Vivek should, 'take down the Ad.' He probably wants a Dumocrat to win, and certainly doesn't want someone who will do a much better job than he is capable of doing. I suggested, on the other hand, that Vivek should keep it up..." Mr. Trump added he only wishes the "mothers of my opponents would be so brave as to come forward and explain that their son or daughter is a liar, and much worse." "Who wouldn't use such an Ad?" Mr. Trump wrote. "I would, it's called, 'hitting pay dirt.'" Mr. Trump continued to defend the ad during a rally in Iowa late Thursday. He said he advised Ramaswamy that "you gotta ride with it," later adding: "Leave it up, and look upstairs and say, 'Thank you God, very much.'" Vance, too, defended the ad, saying Republicans who have criticized it should "stop whining." Ohio Republican Sen. John Husted, who is running for reelection, said he "would not have run that ad." Outgoing Rep. Nancy Mace of South Carolina called the ad the "most shameful, disgusting, offensive ad this election season." Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose, a Republican, told a local ABC station he "probably wouldn't run an ad like that, but every candidate gets to make their own decision." Acton's brother said earlier this week it's "not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at twelve years old from our birth mother's husband into a political talking point." "Our birth mother stayed married to Amy's rapist until he died," Stearns said. "This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core – a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants." This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/ramaswamy-ad-amy-acton-mother-trump/

item.title: DOJ investigating Corey Lewandowski's role in DHS contracting under Kristi Noem
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Corey Lewandowski speaks to the press in July 2024..(Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images) - Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Justice Department prosecutors are investigating allegations of contract misconduct at the Department of Homeland Security, including the role of Corey Lewandowski who worked as de facto chief of staff to former Secretary Kristi Noem, according to multiple people familiar with the investigation. The probe follows a criminal referral for Lewandowski from the DHS Inspector General’s office, which has been examining contracting practices at the agency during Noem’s and Lewandowski’s tenure, according to one of the people familiar. The Justice Department declined to comment on the matter. “Mr. Lewandowski has not been contacted by the Justice Department regarding any investigation, and he denies any wrongdoing when he was proudly serving his country in a voluntary capacity,” Lewandowski’s attorney Adam Trigg told CNN. The Department of Homeland Security didn’t immediately return a request for comment on the matter. The referral is an unusual move for the Trump administration, which has been hesitant to criminally investigate its own members. Critics have instead largely accused the Justice Department of improperly targeting the president’s political enemies and accused DHS of protecting their own employees from scrutiny. In recent months, as the allegations of possible corruption emerged, Washington, DC, US Attorney Jeanine Pirro told officials in her office that she wanted investigators to look into claims of kickbacks connected to contracting at DHS, according to a second source familiar with the investigation. It’s still not clear which US Attorney’s office is leading the investigation. Prosecutors have been awaiting results from the DHS inspector general probe, the person familiar with the probe said. Lewandowski, a Republican operative, became a fixture at DHS early in President Donald Trump’s second term, serving as Noem’s chief adviser. But on paper, he was originally tapped to serve as a special government employee — a unique role meant to span a limited number of days. Lewandowksi’s straddling of senior government functions at DHS and service as a special government employee was uncharted territory, according to multiple people who spoke with CNN. Homeland Security officials ultimately viewed Lewandowski, a Trump ally, as Noem’s gatekeeper. He left the department when Trump fired Noem. Noem’s handling of contracts within DHS was one of the main catalysts for her ouster by Trump earlier this year, notably when she claimed that Trump knew of a $220 million ad campaign prominently featuring the secretary. During her tenure, Noem also tightened her grip on her department’s purse strings, ordering that every contract and grant over $100,000 had to cross her desk for approval — a move that Noem frequently defended as intended to cut down on waste but that multiple Homeland Security officials found unusual and unnecessary. The inspector general, Joseph Cuffari, complained to Congress in early March that Homeland Security leadership had been obstructing some of his work. Trump, when asked by a reporter on Thursday about the Lewandowski investigation, said he didn’t know much about it as he only just learned of it. He repeatedly said, however, that if people working for him are dishonest, he wants them prosecuted. “They’re stealing from me, so I want my people to be honest,” Trump said. “And if they’re not honest, I’ll have my DOJ go and do whatever they have to do.” This story has been updated with additional details.
